lesson.subtitle: Lesson 4 -- If They Ask You That
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Luiz Fernando da Silva | Lesson 4 -- If They Ask You That

listenings.text: I interpret for boards, so I spend my working life watching people who are competent in one language look uncertain in another, and I want to say something about that. The single most common mistake I see is not a grammar mistake. It is somebody who did not catch the question and answers anyway. They give a long answer to a question nobody asked, and the room quietly decides that this person is not on top of the detail. The fix takes four seconds. Ask them to say it again in a different way. Nobody has ever thought less of somebody for asking that. What they think less of is the answer that misses. And here is the part that surprises people. In my experience, senior visitors expect to repeat themselves. They came a long way, they know their accent is not easy, and they would rather explain twice than be agreed with by somebody who did not follow.

When I visit a site as an investor, I am not looking for a presentation. I have read the numbers on the plane. What I am trying to find out in two days is whether the people running the operation know where the problem is. So my questions are usually small and specific, and they sound harmless. How long does that take. Who signs that off. What happens if the customer does not pay in April. And what I am listening for is whether the answer has a number and a date in it, or whether it has adjectives. If somebody tells me the situation is under control, I have learned nothing. If somebody tells me that four accounts are late, that all four are the same kind of customer, and that they will know more after the harvest, then I trust the whole department, including the parts I did not ask about.

reading.rtitle: The Question You Did Not Catch
paras: Every company that receives foreign visitors has the same quiet problem, and almost nobody names it. Somebody senior asks a question across a table, the accent is unfamiliar, the room is noisy, and the person answering catches about seventy per cent of it. What happens next decides how that person is remembered. If they ask for the question again, the meeting loses four seconds. If they answer anyway, they give a long reply to a question that was not asked, and the visitor draws a conclusion that has nothing to do with language.

Interpreters who work with boards say the same thing repeatedly: the people who ask are not the ones who look weak. Senior visitors expect to repeat themselves, because they know their own accent is not easy and they have travelled a long way to hear something accurate. What they cannot use is agreement from somebody who did not follow. So the useful sentences are short and they are always the same three. Ask for it again in different words. Repeat back what you understood. Confirm the number before you commit to it.

The second half of the problem is the answer itself. Visitors ask small, specific questions on purpose, and they are listening for whether the reply contains a number and a date or only adjectives. Under control is not information. Four accounts are late, all four are the same kind of customer, and we will know more after the harvest is information, and it buys trust for the parts of the department nobody asked about. This is why the two skills belong in the same hour: if you do not catch the question, you cannot give the answer that works, and if you cannot give that answer, catching the question was not much use.
